title: Why only 15% of callers leave a voicemail
summary: 85% of callers won’t leave a voicemail, so it’s a poor safety net for missed calls. What happens instead, what to do next, and how to improve.
body_markdown:
Many business owners still treat voicemail as a safety net. In fact, the opposite is true: most callers today won’t leave a voicemail if their call isn’t answered.


In an analysis of over 18 million missed calls in Quo, **only 15% of callers left a voicemail** . Most callers skip the message, assuming that nobody is checking or that another form of communication, like texting, will be faster.


For small businesses, this means the vast majority of missed calls are simply dropping off: no message, no callback request. Often, the caller simply moves on to the next option on their list. In this article, we’ll show you why this happens and what to do about it.


##


Voicemail left rate by industry


From a sample of over 18M missed calls from July to September 2026, only 2.8M ended in a voicemail. That’s more than 8 in 10 callers who hung up at the beep.


Among industries with at least 10,000 missed calls, voicemail left rates ranged from 10% in air freight and logistics to 24% in technology hardware. Here are the five highest and lowest rates, plus how several of the industries we work with most compare:


### Highest voicemail left rates


Tech hardware and insurance had the highest voicemail left rates.


Industry Voicemail left rate


Technology Hardware, Storage, & Peripherals 24%


Insurance 23%

Diversified Financial Services 20%


Accounting 20%


### Lowest voicemail left rates


Air freight and logistics, automotive, and consulting had the lowest voicemail left rates.


Industry Voicemail left rate


Air Freight & Logistics 10%


Automotive 13%


Consulting 13%

Transportation 13%


### Voicemail left rates by popular industries


Industries like legal, finance, and healthcare have higher voicemail rates. This makes sense, as callers have higher stakes, greater sensitivity, and more urgent needs. That said, an 18% voicemail left rate on missed calls still means that the majority of your customers are moving on without you even realizing it.

##


Voicemail left rate by context


When we broke the data down by time of day and type of caller, the pattern stayed mostly the same. Roughly 85% of callers will abandon a call that goes to voicemail.


- **After hours:** 14% of callers left a voicemail
- **Business hours:** 16% left a voicemail
- **First-time callers:** 16% of callers left a voicemail
- **Repeat callers:** 15% left a voicemail


Callers were slightly less likely to leave a voicemail after hours than during business hours, but the gap is small. Even when callers know no one is in the office, most move on.


##


Why people stopped leaving voicemails


So, what happened to voicemail? It likely has nothing to do with your[voicemail greeting](https://www.quo.com/tools/voicemail-generator) . Voicemail expectations and experiences have changed over the last decade.


One reason: there has been a large cultural shift in communication technologies. On personal phones, you can see you missed a call and call them back when you get a chance, no voicemail needed. As a result, many people no longer leave voicemails.


Plus, with caller ID, texting, voice notes, and other convenient ways to communicate, most situations don’t require a voicemail.


Speaking of texting, it’s become the preferred option.[Texting is now the preferred communication channel](https://www.eztexting.com/report/2026-consumer-texting-behavior-report) for 9 of 10 business message categories.


Besides, most of us get voicemails primarily from spam calls. This can prevent people from leaving them or expecting them to be checked. And to be fair, this assumption is partially correct: Our analysis found that[69% never get a callback](https://www.quo.com/blog/small-business-callback-statistics/) within 48 hours.


##


What happens after callers hang up


You may have noticed fewer voicemails lately, but it’s not always clear what’s replacing them. We asked business owners what they saw. Here’s what they told us:


- **Text the business.** When a caller hears the voicemail beep, many hang up and text instead. This is especially true for Millennials and Gen Z, who[default to texting if a call is missed](https://generationallyspeaking.co.uk/generational-communication/) . They text 46% and 53% of the time, respectively.


- **Go to a competitor or the next company.** When customers need an item or service, many aren’t specifically waiting for *your* business. They just need someone who can help. Often, they go to the company that picks up first — or the one with the fastest[speed to lead](https://www.quo.com/blog/speed-to-lead/) . If the call is missed, customers simply hang up and move on to the next option.


- **Call back or call again.** Occasionally, customers might try again later. This is more common with customers who already work with you. For example, they may be waiting for a follow-up confirmation or a service update.


- **Wait for a callback.** Caller ID has taught many people that you don’t need to leave a voicemail. Everyone can see your number, so many people just hang up and wait for a call back. The takeaway: call back *all* missed calls, not just the ones that leave a voicemail.
- **Email or web form.** Some customers skip the phone entirely and send an email or fill out a web form. That’s likely because it seems faster than leaving a voicemail.


If a caller doesn’t leave a voicemail, the best case scenario is that they try another way to contact you. But why risk it when many customers just move on?

##


Voicemail alternatives for small business owners


Instead of relying solely on voicemail to catch missed calls, use one of these options to help make sure every call gets answered the first time.


Voicemail alternatives Pros Cons Average cost


AI receptionist 24/7 coverage for any call volume; can be quickly programmed for a variety of uses Can’t handle high-stakes or highly complex calls $25–$200+ per month, based on volume


Live receptionist Provides a human touch and more flexibility Inconsistent answering; longer on-ramp and training period $300–$600+ per month, based on volume


In-house employee Highest quality of customer service; can learn your business and customers deeply Expensive; requires onboarding and training time $2,800–$4,000+ per month


Auto-reply texts Responds to customers immediately, 24/7; offers a preferred communication channel Not as personalized; can only take care of limited problems $0–$15+ per month


### 1. AI receptionist


An AI receptionist is a software program that can answer calls immediately. It uses large language models, or LLMs, and natural language processing, or NLP, to understand what callers are asking and to respond. It can often make appointments, answer basic questions, and send text messages. It can also be set up to[route the call](https://www.quo.com/product/call-routing/business-hours-call-routing) elsewhere when needed.


**Best for:** Teams that need 24/7 coverage or want to increase lead volume. AI receptionists, like Quo’s[Sona AI agent](https://www.quo.com/sona) , are great for managing lead capture, especially via SMS. It can also text back or route callers to the appropriate team member for quick handling.


**Drawbacks:** An AI receptionist is ultimately a software program, so it can’t solve every problem or address every request.


**Average Cost:** $25–$200+ per month, based on volume. Your first 10 calls with Sona each month are free on any Quo plan.


### 2. Live receptionist


Unlike an[AI phone answering service](https://www.quo.com/blog/best-ai-phone-answering-services/) , a live receptionist means paying a real human to answer your calls. Typically, you’ll provide them with several scripts. You’ll also provide information about your common business questions, workflows, and scheduling tools. The receptionist can then answer questions, schedule appointments, intake new leads, or forward calls to the appropriate inbox.


**Best for:** Teams that want the human touch and can invest time into training and costs.


**Drawbacks:** The biggest drawback between[voicemail vs. answering services](https://www.quo.com/blog/voicemail-vs-answering-service/) is that training a live receptionist can be time-consuming and requires an on-ramp period. Other solutions can start answering calls right away.


**Cost:**[Answering service costs](https://www.quo.com/blog/answering-service-cost/) range from $300–$600+ per month, with plans based on call volume.


### 3. In-house employee


An in-house employee works for you directly and generally fills a secretary or receptionist role. They provide dedicated support, particularly during business hours. They can also learn your business inside and out. A local, in-house receptionist can fulfill other duties and tasks in addition to answering the phone. It’s an expensive but versatile option.


**Best for:** Teams with[high call volume](https://www.quo.com/blog/high-call-volume/) during business hours and high-stakes calls, like legal or healthcare teams.


**Drawbacks:** It’s the most expensive option and requires significant training and a regular salary.


**Cost:**[Typical receptionist salaries](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/office-and-administrative-support/receptionists.htm) in the US range from $34,000 to $48,000 per year, or $2,800–$4,000 per month.


### 4. Auto-reply texts


[Auto-reply texts](https://www.quo.com/blog/texting-auto-reply-examples/) are the fastest and cheapest option. You can set them up in minutes using a business phone platform, and they work instantly, and around the clock. You can use them to let callers know when you’ll call back, what your business hours are, offer resources, or start a new lead form.


Since many callers prefer texting, auto-reply texts offer immediate responses on the caller’s preferred channel.


**Best for:** Teams with consistent call volume during business hours.


**Drawbacks:** Autoreply texts can frustrate callers who want to speak to a team member. They may still cause callers to choose other companies if you don’t follow up quickly. Auto-reply texts also aren’t as personalized as answering the phone.


**Cost:** $0 to $15 per month, depending on the phone system.


##


Stop relying on voicemail: Answer every call with Quo


The data is clear: most callers will hang up rather than leave a voicemail.


That can be up to 85% of leads, customer questions, or upsell opportunities missed. And while you can’t convince customers to start leaving voicemails, you *can* change what happens when you can’t answer the phone.


Whether you use a live answering service, an AI receptionist, hire someone, or send an auto-reply text, the goal is to respond instantly to every caller. That way, you meet their needs and keep them from going to a competitor.
